paragraphs: Considered politically, all three kinds of religion have flaws. The third is so plainly defective that there is no need to discuss its faults at length. Anything that breaks the social bond is worthless; any institution that turns people against themselves serves no purpose here.

The second kind deserves some praise because it joins worship of the gods with respect for the laws. By making the country itself an object of devotion, it teaches citizens that serving the state means serving its protecting deity. This is a form of theocracy in which the prince alone should be pontiff and magistrates alone should be priests. To die for one’s country in such a state is martyrdom; breaking the laws is impiety; and condemning a criminal to public shame means delivering him to divine anger.

Yet this religion is blameworthy because it rests on falsehood and deceit, misleads people, and makes them gullible and superstitious. It replaces true worship with empty ceremonies. It is also exclusive and tyrannical, making people violent and persecuting, so that a nation may breathe only murder and massacre while believing it performs a holy act by killing those who worship differently. Such a people is naturally at war with every other nation, to its own great peril It treats differences of worship as threats to public order It treats differences of worship as threats to public order.

The only kind left is Christianity’s rational, humane religion—not as people practise it today, but as it appears in the Gospel, which is quite different. According to this holy, elevated, true faith, all people are children of one God and recognize one another as siblings. The society that binds them lasts until death.

But because this religion has no particular tie to the political body, it leaves the laws with no more strength than they had before, adding nothing to them. It therefore does nothing to strengthen the bonds of a particular society. Christianity does not attach citizens’ hearts to the state; it turns them away from it and from worldly affairs generally. Nothing could be more contrary to the spirit of society.

People say that a nation of true Christians would be the most perfect society imaginable. There is one serious objection: a society of true Christians would not be a society of human beings. I will go further: despite its perfection, such a society would be neither strongest nor most durable. Because it would be perfect, it would lack the strongest bonds of connection, and that very lack would destroy it.

Individuals might do their duty; the people might obey the laws; their leaders might be fair, their magistrates honest, and their soldiers unafraid of death. Vanity and luxury might be absent. Everything would seem to go well. But let us consider further.

Christianity is a spiritual faith concerned only with heaven; a Christian’s inheritance is not in this world. He does his duty, certainly, but he is deeply indifferent to whether his efforts succeed or fail. If he has nothing to blame himself for, it matters little to him whether things go well or badly here below. If the state prospers, he can hardly rejoice in its happiness for fear of becoming proud of his country’s glory. If it declines, he blesses God for bringing his people low.

Social peace and harmony also require that every citizen, without exception, be an equally good Christian. If even one is ambitious or hypocritical, if there is a Catiline or Cromwell among them, he will surely prey easily on his pious fellow citizens. Christian charity makes it hard to think ill of one’s neighbour. The moment someone discovers how to deceive the majority and receives some public authority, he becomes a dignitary. Christians must not speak badly of those in office; respected in this way, he gains power. Christians must obey higher authorities. If someone entrusted with power abuses it, he becomes the rod God uses to punish his children.

Even if their consciences allowed Christians to expel a usurper, that would break the public peace and lead to violence and bloodshed—hardly consistent with true Christian meekness. And in this valley of misery, does it matter to them whether they are free or enslaved? Their true concern is saving their souls and gaining happiness in another world; to achieve that, they are taught to accept their condition here.

Suppose such a state is forced into war with a neighbouring power. Its citizens might march into battle without trying to flee and perform their duty on the field, but they would have no eagerness to win; they have been taught that dying is better than conquering. What difference does victory or defeat make to them? Imagine the advantage a fierce, passionate enemy could gain over their restraint. Put them against a brave, generous people filled with love of glory and country—say, a truly Christian republic against Sparta or Rome. The Christians would be beaten, routed, and cut down before they knew what was happening; their only protection would be their enemy’s contempt for them. Fabius’s soldiers swore a fine oath: they did not promise to die or to win, but swore they would return victorious, and they kept their promise. Christian troops could not swear this; they would fear putting the Lord their God to the test.

But I have made a mistake by speaking of a Christian republic: one of these terms necessarily excludes the other. Christianity teaches submission and dependence. Its spirit is too favourable to tyrants for them not to take advantage of it. True Christians are made for slavery, they know it, and they never concern themselves with conspiracies or revolts; this passing life means too little to them.

Will someone say that Christians make excellent soldiers? I deny it. Show me your Christian troops! I know of no truly Christian soldiers. Do you name the Crusaders? Whatever their courage, they were far from being Christian citizens. They were the priest’s soldiers, citizens of the Church, fighting for a spiritual homeland that the Church had somehow turned into a worldly one. This was a return to paganism. Since the Gospel founded no national religion, true Christians could never wage a holy war to the faith Their claimed spiritual purpose also serves as political rule.

Christian soldiers under pagan emperors were brave, as every Christian writer assures us—and I believe them. Their courage came from honour or rivalry stirred by the pagan troops. When the emperors became Christian, that rivalry vanished. Once the cross had driven out the eagle, Roman courage disappeared in the empire.

Setting political questions aside, let us return to the question of right and establish the proper principles for this important matter. The social compact gives the sovereign authority only as far as public benefit requires. A subject is therefore not answerable to the sovereign for beliefs that have nothing to do with the community. It matters greatly to the state that each citizen hold a religion that inspires respect for duty. But that religion’s beliefs concern the community only insofar as they affect morals and the obligations people owe their fellow citizens. Beyond that, each person may profess whatever beliefs he wishes, and the sovereign has no right to interfere. It has no authority over the next world; it does not matter to the sovereign what happens to citizens after death, provided they fulfil their duties in this life.

The Marquis d’A. says that in a republic everyone is perfectly free because nobody may harm another. This is the firm boundary of republican liberty, and it could not be stated more exactly. I cannot resist quoting this unpublished manuscript from time to time to honour a respected and distinguished person who preserved his integrity as a citizen while serving in government and adopted the most honest, beneficial policies for his country.

There is therefore a purely civic profession of faith, whose principles the sovereign may establish—not as religious beliefs but as sentiments required by society, without which a person cannot be a good citizen or faithful subject. The sovereign may justly expel someone who refuses these sentiments, but not for impiety: he is unsociable, unable to sincerely value justice or sacrifice his life when duty requires. If someone publicly professes these sentiments and then behaves as though he rejects them, he may justly be put to death for the greatest of crimes: denying what he holds in his heart before the laws in all cases.

When Caesar argued for Catiline, he tried to establish that the soul is mortal. Cato and Cicero did not answer with a philosophical debate. They showed instead that Caesar spoke like a bad citizen and advanced a doctrine dangerous to the state. That was the only matter before Rome’s Senate; theology was not in question in the Senate itself.

The principles of civic religion should be few and simple, stated precisely, with no explanations or commentary. Its positive beliefs should be: that a powerful, intelligent, benevolent, all-knowing, provident deity exists; that there is an afterlife; that the virtuous are rewarded and the wicked punished; and that the social compact and laws are sacred. For a negative belief, I would include only one: persecution is forbidden.

In my view, those who distinguish civil tolerance from religious tolerance are mistaken. We cannot live in sincere peace with people we firmly believe are condemned. To love them would seem to mean hating God for punishing them, so we must either persecute or convert them. Wherever religious persecution exists, it inevitably affects civil government. The sovereign then ceases to be sovereign even in worldly matters: priests become the real masters and kings merely their agents in any way.

Modern governments cannot maintain one exclusive national religion. They must therefore tolerate every religion that is itself tolerant of others, provided its beliefs do not conflict with the duties of a good citizen. Anyone who dares to say, “There is no salvation outside our church,” should be expelled from the state, unless the state itself is religious and its prince a pontiff. This doctrine is useful only under theocracy; everywhere else it is destructive. The reason Henry IV is said to have given for converting to Roman Catholicism should have made an honest person reject that faith—and especially a prince capable of thinking clearly.
